Average remaining life is not a retirement funding deadline: read the period table

Four interactive graphics distinguish a precise population mean, conditional survival to later ages and a separate constant-cash illustration of longer planning horizons.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Public 2022–2024 period life table for Canada, released 13 January 2026, reviewed 25 October 2026. Metadata identifies this period as preliminary even though the selected row STATUS cells are blank. Source sex categories are retained. The age input conditions on reaching that exact birthday; it does not change mortality rates or estimate personal health. Expected remaining life assumes the reference-period mortality schedule continues. Published 95% margins describe uncertainty in the population mean, not the spread of individual lifespans. Conditional-survival ratios use rounded lx counts from a hypothetical radix of 100,000 births, with no derived confidence interval or future mortality improvement. Displayed survival stops at 100 with no assumption that survival becomes zero afterward. The final chart is separate hypothetical arithmetic: constant real annual cash gap times years to a chosen age, zero real return, no tax or payment-timing calculation and no mortality weighting. It is not a recommended funding age or an insurance quote.

The central idea

Life expectancy is an average under a particular mortality schedule. A cash plan still needs explicit later-age scenarios and resources for the years that may extend beyond that average.

01

Condition on the birthday already reached

A retirement plan can run out of years before it runs out of arithmetic. If its final spending date is chosen only because a life-expectancy figure appears nearby, the plan may stop while the underlying life table still contains survivors.

This article uses Canada’s preliminary 2022–2024 period estimates from Statistics Canada Table 13-10-0114-01. At exact age 65, the both-sexes mean remaining life is 20.85 years. This is conditional on reaching 65; it is not obtained by subtracting 65 from life expectancy at birth.

The source definition holds the mortality observed in the reference period across the hypothetical remaining lifetime. Adding 65 gives 85.85 as a conditional mean age under those assumptions. It is a period measure. It does not follow an actual birth cohort into its future or add assumptions about later mortality improvements.

The age control selects the source row for an exact birthday between 55 and 80. It also changes the denominator of the survival calculations. It does not modify anyone’s health, alter the historical mortality schedule or predict how long a reader will live.

02

Read survivor counts as a life-table construction

The table begins with a hypothetical radix of 100,000 live births. Its survivor column records how many remain at each exact age under the table’s schedule. These figures are not counts of respondents, pension members or actual Canadians still alive from a particular group of births.

In the selected both-sexes table, 88,760 survivors reach exact age 65 and 13,600 reach exact age 95. Dividing 13,600 by 88,760 produces a conditional table proportion of about 15.32%. The denominator is the survivors who already reached 65, rather than the original 100,000.

The survival curve repeats that calculation at each later age. Its value is 100% at the conditioning birthday. From age 65, the same table gives approximately 57.15% reaching 85 and 3.53% reaching 100. An average remaining duration does not turn the later proportions into zero.

The threshold bars are nested. A table survivor reaching 95 has also reached 90, so their percentages cannot be added as separate outcomes. The source sex categories are shown separately. No joint-life or couple probability is calculated from them.

03

A narrow confidence interval is not a narrow range of personal lifespans

The published margin for the both-sexes expectation at age 65 is 0.02 years. Applying it to 20.85 gives a 95% interval for that population mean of 20.83 to 20.87 years. The first chart retains those bounds, even though the whiskers are small on its zero-based axis.

Statistics Canada’s life-table methods explain how the published margins support a 95% confidence interval. This describes precision of the estimated mean. It does not say that 95% of individuals will live between those two remaining durations.

It also does not supply uncertainty around the derived survivor ratios. The article therefore shows no invented confidence band around that curve, and it does not reuse the expectation’s margin for a different statistic. The displayed source counts are rounded, so derived ratios should not be treated as exact personal probabilities.

The reference period is preliminary according to metadata note 14, because late death registrations can lead to updates. The individual selected CSV status cells are blank; that does not override the period-level preliminary designation. The release date, reference period and review date remain distinct.

04

Translate a chosen horizon into a separate cash scenario

The final chart introduces an independent hypothetical input: an annual spending gap of CAD 40,000 in constant purchasing power. It applies no real investment return and simply multiplies that gap by the years between the starting age and each chosen endpoint.

From age 65 to 85, twenty years at that gap total CAD 800,000. Extending the endpoint to 95 produces thirty years and CAD 1,200,000. The additional ten years add CAD 400,000 under these deliberately fixed assumptions.

Those balances are not mortality-weighted present values, market quotations or claims about an adequate reserve. They also do not fund every possible lifespan. Their purpose is to expose how a chosen final age changes a simple cash requirement while keeping the statistical evidence separate.

Changing the spending gap changes only this cash chart and its corresponding dollar metric. It does not change the official expectation, its margin or the conditional survival curves. Changing the conditioning age changes the statistical denominator and the length of each cash horizon, with the source period held fixed.

05

Use later-age scenarios without treating one as a guarantee

A household plan needs its own income sources, accessible assets, spending pattern and contingencies. The simple gap here could be replaced by a documented budget, but actual pension payments, tax, returns, care needs and inflation would need a fuller cash model.

Examine what remains available at more than one later age. Identify income that continues for life, cash obligations that can change and resources that might be difficult to turn into spendable money. A positive balance at one endpoint does not settle the years after it.

The plotted curve stops at exact age 100 because that is this article’s display boundary. It does not assume all remaining lives end there or renormalize the surviving fraction away. A longer planning horizon would need to be assessed explicitly.

Finally, retain the table version and revisit the plan when circumstances or source estimates change. A population statistic can clarify the question being asked; it cannot select a personal death date, an insurance price or a universally sufficient retirement deadline.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. The first three figures use a curated preliminary 2022–2024 Statistics Canada period life table, released 13 January 2026. Source expectations and 95% margins are retained; survival ratios are derived from rounded life-table survivor counts without a derived confidence interval. The fourth figure is original hypothetical cash arithmetic, with no mortality weighting or recommended funding age. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. Statistics Canada · Table 13-10-0114-01 ↗

    Released 13 January 2026; public full CSV and metadata checked 25 October 2026. Curated Canada, 2022–2024, source sex categories, survivor counts at ages 55–100 and expectations/margins at ages 55–80: 294 observations. Metadata notes 6, 10, 11 and 14 support conditional ratios, period expectations, 95% margins and preliminary status. Derived ratios have no calculated confidence interval.

  2. Statistics Canada · Methods for Constructing Life Tables ↗

    Official HTML methods reviewed 25 October 2026, particularly the definition of period-table elements and Step 7 on 95% margins. The article does not treat estimation uncertainty as individual lifespan dispersion or add future mortality improvements.
